problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following results (integration constants omitted):*

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)=2\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are linearly independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡2x+2{sin}^{2}⁡2x \\  & =2\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

Let's compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x \\ {u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x(\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+(B-\frac{1}{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|\end{aligned}
$$

If we redefine the arbitrary constant $B$ as

$$
B:=(B-\frac{1}{2})
$$

our general solution becomes

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,{{-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=-x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|.
$$
